messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A more complicated varying intercepts, varying slopes model
parts:
Hi, Shravan. Others can give you better advice than I can, but my quick guess is that you do not want to be parameterizing the covariance matrix piece by piece in this way.  I think it will be much better to just give a prior to the covariance matrix and let it go at that.  Also, I think you might be able to speed your code with some vectorization.
A
On Dec 16, 2013, at 8:29 PM, Shravan Vasishth <vasishth...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thanks to Sergio and Bob, I fit a slightly more complicated model (psycholinguistic models can be quite a bit more complex than this). This one has three contrasts (plus an intercept) and then varying intercepts by subject, and varying slopes, i.e., six correlations and four variance components are estimated for the subject, and of course the variance for the residuals. 

The data are from: http://openscience.uni-leipzig.de/index.php/mr2/article/view/11

I link the data here.

The code is given below. One surprising thing is that Stan runs amazingly slow (MacBook Air OS X 10.6).  I thought Stan was supposed to be fast. Am I doing something wrong? (Bob, I tried to indent the comments, it was OK on my editor, but it got messed up once I copied it into this google groups message window; sorry about that).

## data source:
## http://read.psych.uni-potsdam.de/pmr2/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=10:kliegt-type&catid=11:publications&Itemid=13

library(lme4)
# Various transformations stored in the following data frame
load("KWDYZ_test.rda")

summary(m2 <- lmer(rt ~ 1 + c1 + c2 + c3 + (1 + c1 + c2 + c3 | id), 
                    data=dat))  

library(car)
qqPlot(residuals(m2))

#getME(m2, name="theta")                                                             
#confint(m2, method="boot")  # Takes a long time

## Stan analysis:
dat2 <- list(mu_prior=c(0,0,0,0),
                     id=sort(as.integer(factor(dat$id))),
                     rt = dat$rt,
                     c1 = dat$c1,
                     c2 = dat$c2,
                     c3 = dat$c3,
                     N = nrow(dat),
                     I = length(unique(dat$id)))  


klieglvaryingintslopes_code<- 'data {
int<lower=1> N;
real rt[N];                         //outcome
real c1[N];                         //predictor
real c2[N];                         //predictor
real c3[N];                         //predictor
int<lower=1> I;                     //number of subjects
int<lower=1, upper=I> id[N];        //subject id
vector[4] mu_prior;                 //vector of zeros passed in from R
}
parameters {
vector[4] beta;                     // intercept and slope
vector[4] u[I];                     // random intercept and slopes
real<lower=0> sigma_e;              // residual sd 
vector<lower=0>[4] sigma_u;         // subj sd
corr_matrix[4] Omega;               // correlation matrix for random intercepts and slopes
}
transformed parameters {
cov_matrix[4] Sigma;  // constructing the variance/cov matrix for random effects
for (r in 1:4) {
for (c in 1:4) {
Sigma[r,c] <- sigma_u[r] * sigma_u[c] * Omega[r,c];
}
}
}
model {
real mu[N];                         // mu for likelihood
for (i in 1:I) u[i] ~ multi_normal(mu_prior, Sigma);  
// loop for subj random effects
for (n in 1:N) {
mu[n] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*c1[n] + beta[3]*c2[n] + beta[4]*c3[n] +  u[id[n], 1] + u[id[n], 2]*c1[n] + u[id[n], 3]*c2[n] + u[id[n], 4]*c3[n];
}
rt ~ normal(mu,sigma_e);           // likelihood
beta ~ normal(0,100);
sigma_e ~ cauchy(0,2);
sigma_u ~ cauchy(0,2);
Omega ~ lkj_corr(4.0);
}
generated quantities {
real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho12;
real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho13;
real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho14;
real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho23;
real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho24;
real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho34;
rho12 <- Sigma[1,2] / sqrt(Sigma[1,1] * Sigma[2,2]);
rho13 <- Sigma[1,3] / sqrt(Sigma[1,1] * Sigma[3,3]);
rho14 <- Sigma[1,4] / sqrt(Sigma[1,1] * Sigma[4,4]);
rho23 <- Sigma[2,3] / sqrt(Sigma[2,2] * Sigma[3,3]);
rho24 <- Sigma[2,4] / sqrt(Sigma[2,2] * Sigma[4,4]);
rho34 <- Sigma[3,4] / sqrt(Sigma[3,3] * Sigma[4,4]);
}
'
library(rstan)

set_cppo('fast')

fit <- stan(model_code = klieglvaryingintslopes_code, 
            data = dat2, 
            iter = 1000, chains = 4)

print(fit)

parts:
On 12/16/13, 2:29 PM, Shravan Vasishth wrote:
> Thanks to Sergio and Bob, I fit a slightly more complicated model (psycholinguistic models can be quite a bit more
> complex than this). This one has three contrasts (plus an intercept) and then varying intercepts by subject, and varying
> slopes, i.e., six correlations and four variance components are estimated for the subject, and of course the variance
> for the residuals.
>
> The data are from: http://openscience.uni-leipzig.de/index.php/mr2/article/view/11
>
> I link the data here <https://www.dropbox.com/s/pwuz1g7rtwy17p1/KWDYZ_test.rda>.

>
> The code is given below. One surprising thing is that Stan runs amazingly slow (MacBook Air OS X 10.6). I thought Stan
> was supposed to be fast.

It's all relative to other options. MCMC is quite a bit
slower than optimization-based fits.

Does the model (or its analogue with different priors) run faster in JAGS?
> Am I doing something wrong?

The model looks OK, but you have very fat priors (e.g., normal(0,100)).
Do you really expect coefficients in that range?

Also, are you sure you need 1000 iterations? How fast does it
converge and how many effective samples do you need? When you
compare MCMC algorithms, the only thing that matters is effective
samples per second, not the time per iteration. See the section
in the manual on MCMC analysis if you're not familiar with effective
sample size estimation.

The other thing to do is look at the traceplots. Are any of
the chains getting stuck? Are you exploring unrealistic values?
These can sometimes be controlled by tightening the constraints and/or
priors.

The last thing to do is to reparameterize using a non-centered
parameterization --- see the manual section around the funnel
for both the technique and the motivation. This can make a big
difference in hierarchical models, but it requires more work on
the user's part.

More comments on specific micro-optimizations inline below.

> (Bob, I tried to indent the comments, it was OK on my editor, but
> it got messed up once I copied it into this google groups message window; sorry about that).

Ah --- so that's the culprit. I wonder why some of your lines work and
some don't? I just interact via e-mail.

> ## data source:

>

> int<lower=1> N;
> real rt[N]; //outcome
> real c1[N]; //predictor
> real c2[N]; //predictor
> real c3[N]; //predictor
> int<lower=1> I; //number of subjects

> vector[4] mu_prior; //vector of zeros passed in from R
> }
> parameters {
> vector[4] beta; // intercept and slope
> vector[4] u[I]; // random intercept and slopes
> real<lower=0> sigma_e; // residual sd
> vector<lower=0>[4] sigma_u; // subj sd

> }

> for (r in 1:4) {
> for (c in 1:4) {
> Sigma[r,c] <- sigma_u[r] * sigma_u[c] * Omega[r,c];
> }

You can do half the loop then assign the other half
to the first half to guarantee symmetry and cut down
on auto-diff sizes. For the diagonal, you can use
square(x), which is more efficient than (x * x), though
the square() is not going to make a big difference because
it's only four multiplications.

> }
> model {
> real mu[N]; // mu for likelihood
> for (i in 1:I) u[i] ~ multi_normal(mu_prior, Sigma);
> // loop for subj random effects
> for (n in 1:N) {
> mu[n] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*c1[n] + beta[3]*c2[n] + beta[4]*c3[n] + u[id[n], 1] + u[id[n], 2]*c1[n] + u[id[n], 3]*c2[n]
> + u[id[n], 4]*c3[n];
> }
> rt ~ normal(mu,sigma_e); // likelihood
> beta ~ normal(0,100);
Do you expect betas to be this big?

> sigma_e ~ cauchy(0,2);
> sigma_u ~ cauchy(0,2);

These are also pretty broad priors.

- Bob

messages.author: d4fb714af6c90658
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A more complicated varying intercepts, varying slopes model
parts:
Il 16/12/2013 20:29, Shravan Vasishth ha scritto:
> The code is given below. One surprising thing is that Stan runs
> amazingly slow (MacBook Air OS X 10.6).
You could try parallel sampling. Instead of:

fit <- stan(model_code = klieglvaryingintslopes_code,
data = dat2,
iter = 1000, chains = 4)

try:

library(parallel)
# translate to C++ and compile
sm <- stan_model(model_code = klieglvaryingintslopes_code)
# execute chains in parallel
sflist <- mclapply(1:4, mc.cores = detectCores(),
function(i) sampling(sm, data = dat2,
chains = 1, chain_id = i, iter = 1000,
seed = <an integer>))
# merge
fit <- sflist2stanfit(sflist)

You can save a lot of time even if you just have a dual-core processor.
NB: Setting the seed is "best practice" (i.e. mandatory). Please, read
help(sflist2stanfit).

Sergio

On 12/17/13, 3:59 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Wow, is it that easy to run in parallel? I had no idea! We should put this example in the Rstan start page!

Done.

I'd be careful with that detectCores() operation.
Intel's hyperthreading CPUs overreport number of cores
and usually matching the number of cores is faster
than the number of "hyper" cores. Your mileage may vary.

- Bob
